issues.legal_issue: A special regional and town-planning statute applies when land is acquired to implement a new-town development scheme under that statute.
material_facts: The land was proposed to be acquired to establish a new town.
The State constituted a new-town planning and development authority under the planning statute, and that authority requested acquisition under the statute’s acquisition mechanism.
issues.conclusion: The planning statute applied to the proposed acquisition; the State could not treat the acquisition as governed only by the general acquisition law.
issues.legal_principle: The planning statute applied because the acquisition was sought for planning and development under that statute, and the special authority invoked its acquisition mechanism. The Court distinguished Gandhi Grah Nirman Sahkari Samiti Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan (1993) 2 SCC 662, Pratap v. State of Rajasthan (1996) 3 SCC 1, and Jaipur Development Authority v. Sita Ram (1997) 3 SCC 522 because the Rajasthan statute considered in those cases conferred broader acquisition powers, including acquisition otherwise than at an authority’s request.

predicates.acquisition_challenge: A party challenges a proposed or completed acquisition of land.
predicates.acquisition_for_statutory_new_town: The land is sought for a new town to be planned and developed under a special planning framework.
predicates.special_authority_requested_acquisition: An authority established under that planning framework requested that the land be acquired.

issues.definition: When an acquisition challenge concerns land sought for a new town under a special planning framework and the framework’s authority requested the acquisition, the special planning statute applies.

issues.legal_issue: Only the designated planning board may declare a site for a new town, and it must follow the statutory process for public objections and suggestions before making that declaration.
material_facts: The State did not refer the proposed site to the planning board.
A new-town authority considered sites, selected the proposed site, and recommended acquisition without a declaration by the board.
No declaration of the planning area was made by the board after inviting and considering objections and suggestions.
issues.conclusion: The board alone could declare the site for a new town; the declaration procedure, including consideration of objections and suggestions, was mandatory and had not been followed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 14, 56 and 57 of the Punjab Regional and Town Planning and Development Act, 1995, read together, assign declaration of a planning area—including a site for a new town—to the Board. Section 56 requires publication defining the area, an opportunity to submit objections or suggestions, consideration of those submissions, and a further notification declaring the area. Other authorities may undertake planning and development after the area has been declared, but cannot assume the Board’s declaration function.

rule.if: new_town_planning_proceeding and another_authority_selected_site and board_did_not_declare_area and public_submissions_not_considered

predicates.new_town_planning_proceeding: The proceeding concerns planning and development of a proposed new town.
predicates.another_authority_selected_site: An authority other than the body assigned the declaration function selected or declared the proposed site.
predicates.board_did_not_declare_area: The designated planning board did not declare the proposed area as the site for a new town.
predicates.public_submissions_not_considered: The prescribed opportunity for objections or suggestions was omitted, or the submissions received were not considered by the designated board.

issues.definition: In a new-town planning proceeding, a site selected by another authority without a declaration by the designated board and consideration of public submissions does not satisfy the required declaration procedure.

issues.legal_issue: Acquisition for a new town cannot be justified as serving a public purpose under the planning statute when no planning area has been validly declared.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications stated that the land was required to establish a new town.
No planning area or site for a new town had been validly declared by the competent body.
The acquisition was sought for the purposes of the new-town authority under the planning statute.
issues.conclusion: There was no valid public purpose for the acquisition, and the acquisition notifications could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Section 42 of the Punjab Regional and Town Planning and Development Act, 1995 permits acquisition for the purposes of an authority under that Act. Because the planning area had not been validly declared under Section 56, there was no validly selected site to develop and no basis for invoking Section 42 for this new-town scheme. The Court distinguished Ajay Krishan Shinghal v. Union of India (1996) 10 SCC 721: the issue was not whether a broadly stated planned-development purpose needed further particulars in an acquisition notification, but whether a valid planning area existed at all.

predicates.acquisition_challenge: A party challenges an acquisition of land.
predicates.acquisition_for_new_town: The land is proposed to be acquired to establish or develop a new town.
predicates.no_valid_planning_area: The competent body has not validly declared the area for the proposed development.

issues.definition: An acquisition for a new town lacks a valid public purpose when the area for that town has not been validly declared.

issues.legal_issue: The State’s general power to acquire land does not permit it to bypass mandatory procedures governing a scheme implemented under a special planning statute.
material_facts: The State sought to acquire land to implement a new-town scheme governed by the planning statute.
The State relied on its general acquisition power despite the absence of the planning statute’s required declaration of a planning area.
The State had not called on the planning board to select a site, and another authority undertook that task instead.
issues.conclusion: For this acquisition under the new-town scheme, the State had to follow the planning statute’s mandatory procedure and could not rely on its general acquisition power to avoid it.
issues.legal_principle: The State’s power of eminent domain does not displace the procedure prescribed by the Punjab Regional and Town Planning and Development Act, 1995 when acquisition is sought to implement a scheme under that Act. Section 42 permits acquisition on the authority’s request for the authority’s purposes, while Sections 14 and 56 provide for the Board’s role in selecting and declaring a planning area. Gandhi Grah Nirman Sahkari Samiti Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan (1993) 2 SCC 662, and the cases following it, were distinguishable because the Rajasthan statute allowed acquisition on broader terms, including otherwise than on an authority’s request.

predicates.acquisition_challenge: A party challenges an acquisition of land.
predicates.acquisition_under_special_planning_schem: The acquisition is sought to implement a development scheme governed by a special planning framework.
predicates.mandatory_planning_procedure_bypassed: The State proceeds with acquisition without following a procedure required for the scheme under that framework.

issues.definition: When acquisition is sought to implement a scheme governed by a special planning framework, the State cannot use its general acquisition power to bypass that framework’s mandatory procedure.

issues.legal_issue: Adverse observations suggesting mala fides must be set aside when the record does not support them.
material_facts: The High Court had declined to find mala fides but made adverse observations about the State’s conduct.
The record showed that the State acted with haste and failed to observe mandatory planning provisions, but did not justify the adverse observations suggesting mala fides.
issues.conclusion: The adverse observations concerning mala fides were set aside because the material on record did not justify them.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held, on its assessment of the record, that haste and failure to comply with mandatory provisions did not justify the High Court’s adverse observations about mala fides. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.state_appeal: The State appeals from a judgment containing adverse observations about its conduct.
predicates.adverse_mala_fide_observations: The judgment makes observations suggesting that the State acted with mala fides.
predicates.record_does_not_support_mala_fides: The evidence in the record does not justify the suggestion of mala fides.

issues.definition: When the State appeals from adverse observations suggesting mala fides and the record does not support that suggestion, those observations are set aside.
